tone_statements.citation: Ebarb, Kristopher J., Christopher R. Green & Michael R. Marlo. 2014. Luyia tone melodies. Africana Linguistica 20: 121-143.
tone_statements.quote: In all Luyia languages, verb inflection is characterized by distinctive ‘ melodic H’ (H M ) tones on specific positions of the (macro) stem. … Reversive languages, like Bukusu and Nyala‑East, are geographically and, we hypothesize, historically intermediate between conservative and predictable varieties. Forms in (2) show that, like conservative languages, reversive systems retain a two‑way tone distinction in verb roots, but like predictable languages, all verbs have a H M . (2) Nyala‑East (reversive) * Ø verbs a‑lá[ kúlíx‑á] ‘ he will name’ * H verbs a‑lá[ xalák‑á] ‘ he will cut’
tone_statements.locator: pp. 122-123, sec. 1 Introduction, ex. (2) on p. 123

tone_statements.citation: Etakwa, Everlyn. 2010. A phonological analysis of the constraints on the syllable structures of Olunyala. MA thesis (English and Linguistics), Kenyatta University, Nairobi. (KU Institutional Repository handle 123456789/516, issued 2011-07-27; thesis dated March 2010.)
tone_statements.quote: In his study on Verb Tonology in Olunyala (B), Onyango, (2006) concludes that in Olunyala, the number of syllables in the verb affects its tonal pattern. Onyango (Ibid) also shows how the CV syllable structure in Olunyala is preserved in tone allocation. The issue of the preservation of the CV syllable structure was used to investigate if the preferred syllable structure in Olunyala was CV or V. As pointed out in section 1.1, both Olunyala (K) and (B) are closely related and so Onyango s findings on tone apply to Olunyala (K).
tone_statements.locator: ch. 2 literature review, section on studies of Luyia dialects, pp. 19-20
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: None given; treats Olunyala (K) as tonal by extension from West Nyala verb tonology (Onyango 2006).

sources.note: East Nyala lists only Möhlig 1985 and Odden 2009 (subclassification) plus the two theses; West Nyala (Busia, Lake Victoria shore) cites Ochwaya-Oluoch 2003 pp. 7-8 for the two Nyalas being 'not mutually intelligible'. sources.citation: Osotsi, Eric M. 2020. A Systematic Reconstruction of the Phonology of Proto-Luyia: A Comparative Analysis. MA thesis, University of Nairobi. 127 pp.http://hdl.handle.net/11295/154048
sources.note: Sections 2.2.3 (pp. 21-22) and 2.3.3 (p. 28) give only the segmental phonemic inventory of 'Lunyala East' (24 consonants, 7 vowels); the whole thesis has no mention of stress, accent, prosody or suprasegmentals, and tone is mentioned only for Lubukusu dialects (p. ~12). Silent on stress.

tone.says: Bantu (Luyia) tone system of the 'reversive' type: verb roots keep a two-way lexical contrast (toneless vs. high) and every verb form also carries an inflectional melodic high tone.
